summary.oneLiner: The quarter's headline is that the **Energy Solutions platform stopped being an incubation line item and became a fourth business**: ₹590cr EBIT (₹570cr of it from the long-term supply position, ₹1,838cr revenue on 3,325 MUs), on the back of ~5 GW of take-or-pay green supply plus 3,500 MWh of contracted battery storage. The catch is candid and repeated by management — **the purchase side is locked long-term, the sale side is not yet**, so this quarter's spread is partly a hot-summer/delayed-monsoon merchant windfall. The forward test is simple: do the "very advanced stage" long-term offtake contracts land and convert this into annuity, or does the ₹590cr prove to be a seasonal peak?
summary.business: Adani Energy Solutions Limited (formerly Adani Transmission Limited) is an integrated power infrastructure company operating power transmission networks, transmission & distribution services, and smart electricity metering, along with limited power trading and renewable generation. It serves B2B customers (power generation, transmission & distribution, smart metering) and B2C retail electricity consumers through its distribution arms Adani Electricity Mumbai Limited (AEML) and MPSEZ Utilities Limited (MUL), with a pan-India presence spanning 16 states.

Transmission: Power transmission network and related ancillary services
Transmission & Distribution: Transmission and distribution network; retail sale of power to household, industrial and commercial consumers
Smart Metering: Smart electricity metering as a service
Renewable Energy: Wind and solar power generation sold through Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs)

endMarkets: 16 Indian states (Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Delhi, Gujarat, Haryana, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal), including the Mundra and Mumbai distribution license areas|Domestic India only — no export turnover during the reporting period

currentContext.strengths: Only private-sector player in India with HVDC (High Voltage Direct Current) transmission capability
currentContext.strategies: Group (including ADANIENSOL) is shifting from a period of rapid capital expansion to disciplined execution, embedding a three-layer, flattened organisational structure to speed up decision-making and capital deployment.|ADANIENSOL positions itself at the centre of India's energy transition through its portfolio of transmission, distribution, smart metering, centralised cooling and an integrated energy-solutions platform.|Maintain and extend leadership as India's only private-sector player with HVDC transmission capability.|Adani Cooling Solutions is building toward a market-leading centralised/district cooling position, offering Cooling-as-a-Service (CaaS) under a DBFOO model that removes upfront capex for customers across commercial real estate, data centres, airports, industrial estates and townships.|Cooling Solutions strategy targets high-demand urban clusters with a disciplined market approach, emphasising efficient technologies and early-mover advantage in an under-penetrated sector.|Continued focus on completing marquee cooling projects at Shantigram and Mundra SEZ as the cooling solutions business scales.|Board has chosen not to recommend any dividend for FY26, judging it prudent given the tremendous growth/capex opportunities the Company is currently pursuing, i.e. a reinvestment-over-payout posture; no amount was transferred to General Reserves either. A formal Dividend Distribution and Shareholder Return Policy (under SEBI LODR Reg. 43A) exists and is published on the Company's website.
currentContext.expansion: AESL continued to scale its transmission platform during FY26, positioning itself as holding nearly one-fifth of India's private transmission network. Five transmission projects were commissioned during the year: Sangod Transmission, Khavda Phase-II Part-A and the Khavda Pooling Station-1 (commissioned in Q1), followed by additional network additions on the North Karanpura transmission line, culminating in the commissioning of the landmark Mumbai HVDC project (Mumbai's first advanced VSC-based HVDC installation). The company also secured the Khavda South Olpad HVDC line, reinforcing its position as the only private-sector player in India with HVDC capability. The transmission order book rose from Rs 59,936 crore to Rs 71,779 crore over the year. At the site/equipment level, the company commissioned a 12 Ohm series reactor in Mahendragarh, established a 4x500MVA, 400/220kV Jam Khambhaliya substation (GIS) in Gujarat under Jam Khambhaliya Transco Limited, and installed an additional 3.3 MW of solar capacity across Akola, Koradi, Mahendragarh, Rajnandangaon, Sami and Warangal sites (with Rs 0.43 crore capital investment on energy-conservation equipment during the year). Forward-looking strategic priorities identified include smart metering and digital grid expansion, development of green transmission corridors to evacuate renewable capacity, and strengthening internal capital classification/reporting to better track sustainability-linked R&D and capex spend in future reporting cycles.
currentContext.mdna: India's electricity consumption is expected to grow significantly, supported by rising electrification, urbanisation and emerging demand from data centres and digital infrastructure.|Installed capacity is projected to approach ~1,000 GW by FY 2031-32, with investments exceeding USD 500 billion across the energy value chain.|Renewable energy targets of 500 GW by 2030 are increasing the need for robust transmission networks and flexible grid management.|Peak demand is expected to rise to ~388 GW by FY 2031-32, requiring a balanced mix of baseload and renewable capacity, creating opportunities across transmission expansion, distribution privatisation, smart metering adoption and newer solutions such as cooling and integrated energy services.|The global energy landscape is shifting from a molecular energy paradigm (coal, oil, gas) to an electron-based system (electricity), with electrification replacing combustion-based systems across cooking, mobility and industrial processes, also reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels.|India's cooling market remains significantly under-penetrated despite strong structural drivers (urbanisation, rising incomes, expanding real estate, high ambient temperatures); cooling demand, led by space cooling, is projected to multiply over the next decade.|Policy frameworks such as the India Cooling Action Plan (ICAP) 2019 and District Cooling Guidelines 2023 are pushing energy-efficient, centralised cooling solutions including district cooling and thermal energy storage.|Centralised cooling in India remains at a nascent stage with limited domestic competition and dominance of international players, presenting an early-mover opportunity for the company.|Transmission order book rose from Rs 59,936 crore to Rs 71,779 crore during the year.|Sector-wide transmission pipeline of over Rs 9.15 trillion, with a near-term tendering opportunity of ~Rs 1.50 trillion.|Cooling Solutions: ~76,000 TR of projects set to commission and 76,782 TR of projects under implementation, with a broader pipeline of ~266,325 TR across real estate, airports, IT hubs, industrial estates, data centres and metro rail projects.

one-line thesis: The quarter's headline is that the **Energy Solutions platform stopped being an incubation line item and became a fourth business**: ₹590cr EBIT (₹570cr of it from the long-term supply position, ₹1,838cr revenue on 3,325 MUs), on the back of ~5 GW of take-or-pay green supply plus 3,500 MWh of contracted battery storage. The catch is candid and repeated by management — **the purchase side is locked long-term, the sale side is not yet**, so this quarter's spread is partly a hot-summer/delayed-monsoon merchant windfall. The forward test is simple: do the "very advanced stage" long-term offtake contracts land and convert this into annuity, or does the ₹590cr prove to be a seasonal peak?
financial scorecard (q1 fy27):
| Metric | Q1FY27 | YoY | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | not quantified on call (referred to presentation) | — | Energy Solutions split given: long-term PPA **₹1,838cr**, power-mgmt services **₹16cr**, C&I merchant + trading **₹12cr** |
| EBITDA / margin | not given on call | — | Energy Solutions **EBIT ₹590cr** (₹570cr from the contracted-position book) |
| PAT (rptd & normalized) | not given on call | — | — |
| Gross margin | services spread **~₹0.03/unit** (Paisa 3) on the solutioning leg | — | position-taking leg materially higher, contract-by-contract |
| Order book | Smart meters: **1.34cr installed of 2.46cr order book**; +IntelliSmart takes combined portfolio to **~4.7cr (47mn) meters** | — | contract has provisions for natural volume growth beyond 4.7cr |
| Cash / net debt | not disclosed on call | — | stated focus on "reducing cost of capital and improving credit quality" |
> Adjustments / one-offs: (a) **smart-metering segment optically declined QoQ** in the presentation — this is an accounting artefact of the conventional method (construction capex booked as both expense and revenue); the *operating* revenue from commissioned meters actually rose **₹68cr → ₹161cr** QoQ, because only 21 lakh meters were installed this quarter (lower capex). (b) Energy Solutions margins were **inflated by delayed monsoon** — high demand, high market prices; management explicitly flagged both YoY and QoQ variability if positions stay open. Quarterly capex ~**₹3,500cr**.
guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- **Order/capex inflow:** ~25% market share of transmission bidding maintained → **₹20,000–25,000cr of capex addition every year**. Bidding opportunity seen at "minimum ₹1 lakh crore" p.a. (central + state combined); **STU pipeline alone ~₹20,000–25,000cr/yr**.
- **HVDC commissioning:** **KPS-1 ≈ December FY29**; **Rajasthan (Bhadla–Fatehpur) at the beginning of FY29**. Two more HVDC projects — one under bidding, one going to bid shortly.
- **Energy Solutions:** market opportunity being targeted = **7.5 GW+ by 2031** (per company presentation); C&I market seen at 50 GW+ by 2030–31.
- **Sale-side tie-up:** long-term offtake contracts "in very advanced stage" to cover most of the ~5 GW purchase position — barring "a few percentage of capacity that will remain liquid," everything to be tied back-to-back.
- **IntelliSmart:** before CCI; on approval, combined meter portfolio **~4.7cr**, return profile "more or less on similar line" to AESL.
- Smart-meter balance tender opportunity in the market: **10–11cr (100–120mn) meters** (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana, part Andhra + part-quantum states).
order book & pipeline:
- Transmission: **~28,000 ckm** of lines operating. Growth "locked in"; ₹3,500cr of capex deployed in the quarter alone.
- STU (state transmission utility) is called out as the *new* pipeline leg: after 4–5 years of inter-state lines delivering power *to* states, states must now augment intra-state capacity. Maharashtra "very active"; Rajasthan and UP started. Payment mechanism is stated to be **identical to CTU at central level** — STU bills DISCOMs monthly and pays transmission companies.
- HVDC demand is now also arising from **load centres** (city cores where overhead lines are impossible), citing last year's Mumbai HVDC as the proof point.
- Smart metering: 1.34cr installed / 2.46cr ordered; +IntelliSmart.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Energy Solutions** is two distinct businesses: (i) **supply/consumption stack** — ~5 GW of take-or-pay renewable supply (**~4 GW from AGEL, balance third party**, price discovery market-linked) + **3,500 MWh of contracted BESS on fixed hire**, sold to data centres, utilities and C&I under long-term take-or-pay; this is the EBITDA generator (₹570cr of the ₹590cr). (ii) **services/trading** — managing customers' power loads and exchange trading; high volume (9,800 MUs), thin spread (~₹0.03/unit), ₹16cr + ₹12cr revenue.
- Total units handled **13,181 MUs** in the quarter; 3,325 MUs in the position book of which only ~400–500 MUs sit against the 350 MW of signed C&I customers — i.e. **the majority was still sold short-term/on exchange or bilaterally** (contract tenors 1–13 months, prices ₹3 to ₹13–15/unit incl. bundled product).
- **Distribution + smart metering** described as growing at a "stable pace"; transmission and energy solutions delivered the growth.
- Parallel-licence applications: **still pending with the commission, no movement** — Maharashtra government has advised the commission to wait for the central tariff-policy amendment.
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Data centres** are today negligible (one contract, ~20–25 MW serviced) but framed as the big forward volume: every 1 GW of IT load ≈ 1.5x consumption load, and to serve that from renewables needs **3.5–4x renewable capacity plus significant storage**. All Indian data centres are grid/on-grid, not off-grid.
- **Utilities moving to RTC/complex solutions**: DISCOMs are shifting from buying solar/wind/storage separately (which has slipped on delivery) to bundled round-the-clock solutions — precisely the AESL Energy Solutions product.
- **Enabling capex** on last-mile connectivity for consumers/generators — not a capex-led business, but AESL earns a margin on the transmission infra it builds to enable each transaction.
- **MSEDCL 2.5 GW RTC** (LOI to Adani Power): management says group-level solutioning is neutral to AESL and **"AESL will be a major participant in that contract."**
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **~25% sustained market share** in transmission bidding, with the stated intent to at least hold it — the basis for the ₹20–25k cr/yr capex guidance.
- **Right-of-way execution** is treated as a proprietary capability, not a systemic excuse: ROW decisions are pushed to ground level and worked "in parallel" rather than depending 100% on state machinery; projects are geographically clustered where AESL already has presence, so problems are known in advance. Management claims "a little better effectiveness" than industry.
- **Scale-driven cost position in metering**: capex *and* opex per meter reduced over two years using scale — the same advantage is expected to carry into the IntelliSmart volume.
- Being a transmission company, providing last-mile infra to C&I customers is "natural to us" — a structural cross-sell no pure trader can replicate.
margins & cost dynamics:
- Energy Solutions margin has two very different profiles: **services ≈ ₹0.03/unit** (essentially a fee, volumes irrelevant) versus **position-taking contracts at materially higher, contract-specific spreads**.
- The Q1 spread was helped by **delayed monsoon → high demand → high market prices**. Management pre-empted the sustainability question directly: keeping 100% of the position open imports year-to-year *and* quarter-to-quarter volatility (summer > monsoon > winter, with irrigation-demand months distorting further). Stated strategy: close both sides without much time lag and take only limited market exposure.
- Smart metering: reduced installation volume (21 lakh meters this quarter) mechanically reduces the accounting revenue/EBITDA even as the annuity from commissioned meters rises.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **₹3,500cr capex delivered in the quarter** — the stated operating discipline is to convert "locked-in opportunity on the ground" project by project.
- HVDC: KPS-1 → ~Dec FY29; Rajasthan → early FY29. **These are the two dates to check against slippage each quarter.**
- Guided run-rate of **₹20,000–25,000cr capex addition p.a.** from new wins.
capital allocation:
- Explicit framing: maintain *execution* discipline **and** *capital* discipline through a high-growth period, so as to reduce cost of capital and improve credit quality — described as "our focus going forward."
- IntelliSmart is the only announced inorganic move; awaiting CCI.
- No dividend/buyback discussion on this call.
risks & watch-items:
1. **Open sale-side position in Energy Solutions.** ~5 GW purchased on take-or-pay against only 350 MW of contracted C&I; the balance is being placed short-term. If the "advanced stage" long-term contracts don't sign, a soft power market turns a fixed cost into a P&L hit.
2. **Seasonality/merchant price dependence** — Q1 benefited from delayed monsoon; monsoon and winter quarters are structurally weaker on merchant rates.
3. **Right-of-way** is acknowledged as a live, industry-wide ground problem.
4. **Parallel-licence stalemate** in Maharashtra — pending the central tariff-policy amendment, no movement, and no timeline offered.
5. **CCI approval risk/timing** on IntelliSmart; the 4.7cr combined meter portfolio is not yet owned.
6. **Related-party optics**: ~4 GW of the 5 GW supply stack is from AGEL, and AESL expects to buy from Adani Power to serve the MSEDCL contract. Management stated price discovery is market-linked, but the concentration is real.
management quality / tone: Confident and unusually specific on the *mechanics* of the new business — Raj Kumar Jain walked the revenue/cost/capex stack of Energy Solutions end-to-end when asked, and both he and the CEO volunteered the variability risk rather than being pushed to it ("this is a very relevant and very important question"). Where numbers weren't available they declined rather than improvised (contract-specific spreads, exact bilateral pricing). Kandarp Patel's framing — "AESL has arrived as a full-scale utility platform" — is promotional, but it is backed by four disclosed segment P&Ls rather than a slogan.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The **13,181 MU total handled vs 3,325 MU in the position book** is the tell: ~75% of throughput is low-margin services/trading. Do not extrapolate the ₹590cr EBIT off total volumes.
- **Adani Green does not sell to data centres at all** — it contracts long-term with SECI/DISCOMs/third parties. AESL is a *customer* of AGEL, and management confirmed that **essentially all group C&I exposure will route through Energy Solutions**, making AESL the group's single commercial front-end for C&I power.
- Management explicitly refused the analyst's arithmetic on 7.5 GW ("7.5 × 24 × 365") — it is a **market-opportunity number, not a contracted volume**, and mixes consumer stacks. Treat it as TAM framing.
- The smart-meter reporting inversion (accounting revenue falling while operating revenue more than doubles) will recur every quarter that installation pace slows — read the press release, not the presentation, for the annuity.

| Cash / net debt | not disclosed on call | — | stated focus on "reducing cost of capital and improving credit quality" |
> Adjustments / one-offs: (a) **smart-metering segment optically declined QoQ** in the presentation — this is an accounting artefact of the conventional method (construction capex booked as both expense and revenue); the *operating* revenue from commissioned meters actually rose **₹68cr → ₹161cr** QoQ, because only 21 lakh meters were installed this quarter (lower capex). (b) Energy Solutions margins were **inflated by delayed monsoon** — high demand, high market prices; management explicitly flagged both YoY and QoQ variability if positions stay open. Quarterly capex ~**₹3,500cr**.
guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- **Order/capex inflow:** ~25% market share of transmission bidding maintained → **₹20,000–25,000cr of capex addition every year**. Bidding opportunity seen at "minimum ₹1 lakh crore" p.a. (central + state combined); **STU pipeline alone ~₹20,000–25,000cr/yr**.
- **HVDC commissioning:** **KPS-1 ≈ December FY29**; **Rajasthan (Bhadla–Fatehpur) at the beginning of FY29**. Two more HVDC projects — one under bidding, one going to bid shortly.
- **Energy Solutions:** market opportunity being targeted = **7.5 GW+ by 2031** (per company presentation); C&I market seen at 50 GW+ by 2030–31.
- **Sale-side tie-up:** long-term offtake contracts "in very advanced stage" to cover most of the ~5 GW purchase position — barring "a few percentage of capacity that will remain liquid," everything to be tied back-to-back.
- **IntelliSmart:** before CCI; on approval, combined meter portfolio **~4.7cr**, return profile "more or less on similar line" to AESL.
- Smart-meter balance tender opportunity in the market: **10–11cr (100–120mn) meters** (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Telangana, part Andhra + part-quantum states).
order book & pipeline:
- Transmission: **~28,000 ckm** of lines operating. Growth "locked in"; ₹3,500cr of capex deployed in the quarter alone.
- STU (state transmission utility) is called out as the *new* pipeline leg: after 4–5 years of inter-state lines delivering power *to* states, states must now augment intra-state capacity. Maharashtra "very active"; Rajasthan and UP started. Payment mechanism is stated to be **identical to CTU at central level** — STU bills DISCOMs monthly and pays transmission companies.
- HVDC demand is now also arising from **load centres** (city cores where overhead lines are impossible), citing last year's Mumbai HVDC as the proof point.
- Smart metering: 1.34cr installed / 2.46cr ordered; +IntelliSmart.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Energy Solutions** is two distinct businesses: (i) **supply/consumption stack** — ~5 GW of take-or-pay renewable supply (**~4 GW from AGEL, balance third party**, price discovery market-linked) + **3,500 MWh of contracted BESS on fixed hire**, sold to data centres, utilities and C&I under long-term take-or-pay; this is the EBITDA generator (₹570cr of the ₹590cr). (ii) **services/trading** — managing customers' power loads and exchange trading; high volume (9,800 MUs), thin spread (~₹0.03/unit), ₹16cr + ₹12cr revenue.
- Total units handled **13,181 MUs** in the quarter; 3,325 MUs in the position book of which only ~400–500 MUs sit against the 350 MW of signed C&I customers — i.e. **the majority was still sold short-term/on exchange or bilaterally** (contract tenors 1–13 months, prices ₹3 to ₹13–15/unit incl. bundled product).
- **Distribution + smart metering** described as growing at a "stable pace"; transmission and energy solutions delivered the growth.
- Parallel-licence applications: **still pending with the commission, no movement** — Maharashtra government has advised the commission to wait for the central tariff-policy amendment.
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Data centres** are today negligible (one contract, ~20–25 MW serviced) but framed as the big forward volume: every 1 GW of IT load ≈ 1.5x consumption load, and to serve that from renewables needs **3.5–4x renewable capacity plus significant storage**. All Indian data centres are grid/on-grid, not off-grid.
- **Utilities moving to RTC/complex solutions**: DISCOMs are shifting from buying solar/wind/storage separately (which has slipped on delivery) to bundled round-the-clock solutions — precisely the AESL Energy Solutions product.
- **Enabling capex** on last-mile connectivity for consumers/generators — not a capex-led business, but AESL earns a margin on the transmission infra it builds to enable each transaction.
- **MSEDCL 2.5 GW RTC** (LOI to Adani Power): management says group-level solutioning is neutral to AESL and **"AESL will be a major participant in that contract."**
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **~25% sustained market share** in transmission bidding, with the stated intent to at least hold it — the basis for the ₹20–25k cr/yr capex guidance.
- **Right-of-way execution** is treated as a proprietary capability, not a systemic excuse: ROW decisions are pushed to ground level and worked "in parallel" rather than depending 100% on state machinery; projects are geographically clustered where AESL already has presence, so problems are known in advance. Management claims "a little better effectiveness" than industry.
- **Scale-driven cost position in metering**: capex *and* opex per meter reduced over two years using scale — the same advantage is expected to carry into the IntelliSmart volume.
- Being a transmission company, providing last-mile infra to C&I customers is "natural to us" — a structural cross-sell no pure trader can replicate.
margins & cost dynamics:
- Energy Solutions margin has two very different profiles: **services ≈ ₹0.03/unit** (essentially a fee, volumes irrelevant) versus **position-taking contracts at materially higher, contract-specific spreads**.
- The Q1 spread was helped by **delayed monsoon → high demand → high market prices**. Management pre-empted the sustainability question directly: keeping 100% of the position open imports year-to-year *and* quarter-to-quarter volatility (summer > monsoon > winter, with irrigation-demand months distorting further). Stated strategy: close both sides without much time lag and take only limited market exposure.
- Smart metering: reduced installation volume (21 lakh meters this quarter) mechanically reduces the accounting revenue/EBITDA even as the annuity from commissioned meters rises.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **₹3,500cr capex delivered in the quarter** — the stated operating discipline is to convert "locked-in opportunity on the ground" project by project.
- HVDC: KPS-1 → ~Dec FY29; Rajasthan → early FY29. **These are the two dates to check against slippage each quarter.**
- Guided run-rate of **₹20,000–25,000cr capex addition p.a.** from new wins.
capital allocation:
- Explicit framing: maintain *execution* discipline **and** *capital* discipline through a high-growth period, so as to reduce cost of capital and improve credit quality — described as "our focus going forward."
- IntelliSmart is the only announced inorganic move; awaiting CCI.
- No dividend/buyback discussion on this call.
risks & watch-items:
1. **Open sale-side position in Energy Solutions.** ~5 GW purchased on take-or-pay against only 350 MW of contracted C&I; the balance is being placed short-term. If the "advanced stage" long-term contracts don't sign, a soft power market turns a fixed cost into a P&L hit.
2. **Seasonality/merchant price dependence** — Q1 benefited from delayed monsoon; monsoon and winter quarters are structurally weaker on merchant rates.
3. **Right-of-way** is acknowledged as a live, industry-wide ground problem.
4. **Parallel-licence stalemate** in Maharashtra — pending the central tariff-policy amendment, no movement, and no timeline offered.
5. **CCI approval risk/timing** on IntelliSmart; the 4.7cr combined meter portfolio is not yet owned.
6. **Related-party optics**: ~4 GW of the 5 GW supply stack is from AGEL, and AESL expects to buy from Adani Power to serve the MSEDCL contract. Management stated price discovery is market-linked, but the concentration is real.
management quality / tone: Confident and unusually specific on the *mechanics* of the new business — Raj Kumar Jain walked the revenue/cost/capex stack of Energy Solutions end-to-end when asked, and both he and the CEO volunteered the variability risk rather than being pushed to it ("this is a very relevant and very important question"). Where numbers weren't available they declined rather than improvised (contract-specific spreads, exact bilateral pricing). Kandarp Patel's framing — "AESL has arrived as a full-scale utility platform" — is promotional, but it is backed by four disclosed segment P&Ls rather than a slogan.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The **13,181 MU total handled vs 3,325 MU in the position book** is the tell: ~75% of throughput is low-margin services/trading. Do not extrapolate the ₹590cr EBIT off total volumes.
- **Adani Green does not sell to data centres at all** — it contracts long-term with SECI/DISCOMs/third parties. AESL is a *customer* of AGEL, and management confirmed that **essentially all group C&I exposure will route through Energy Solutions**, making AESL the group's single commercial front-end for C&I power.
- Management explicitly refused the analyst's arithmetic on 7.5 GW ("7.5 × 24 × 365") — it is a **market-opportunity number, not a contracted volume**, and mixes consumer stacks. Treat it as TAM framing.
- The smart-meter reporting inversion (accounting revenue falling while operating revenue more than doubles) will recur every quarter that installation pace slows — read the press release, not the presentation, for the annuity.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Adani Energy Solutions Limited (formerly Adani Transmission Limited) is an integrated power infrastructure company operating power transmission networks, transmission & distribution services, and smart electricity metering, along with limited power trading and renewable generation. It serves B2B customers (power generation, transmission & distribution, smart metering) and B2C retail electricity consumers through its distribution arms Adani Electricity Mumbai Limited (AEML) and MPSEZ Utilities Limited (MUL), with a pan-India presence spanning 16 states.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's electricity consumption is expected to grow significantly, supported by rising electrification, urbanisation and emerging demand from data centres and digital infrastructure.
- Installed capacity is projected to approach ~1,000 GW by FY 2031-32, with investments exceeding USD 500 billion across the energy value chain.
- Renewable energy targets of 500 GW by 2030 are increasing the need for robust transmission networks and flexible grid management.
- Peak demand is expected to rise to ~388 GW by FY 2031-32, requiring a balanced mix of baseload and renewable capacity, creating opportunities across transmission expansion, distribution privatisation, smart metering adoption and newer solutions such as cooling and integrated energy services.
- The global energy landscape is shifting from a molecular energy paradigm (coal, oil, gas) to an electron-based system (electricity), with electrification replacing combustion-based systems across cooking, mobility and industrial processes, also reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels.
- India's cooling market remains significantly under-penetrated despite strong structural drivers (urbanisation, rising incomes, expanding real estate, high ambient temperatures); cooling demand, led by space cooling, is projected to multiply over the next decade.
- Policy frameworks such as the India Cooling Action Plan (ICAP) 2019 and District Cooling Guidelines 2023 are pushing energy-efficient, centralised cooling solutions including district cooling and thermal energy storage.
- Centralised cooling in India remains at a nascent stage with limited domestic competition and dominance of international players, presenting an early-mover opportunity for the company.
- Transmission order book rose from Rs 59,936 crore to Rs 71,779 crore during the year.
- Sector-wide transmission pipeline of over Rs 9.15 trillion, with a near-term tendering opportunity of ~Rs 1.50 trillion.
- Cooling Solutions: ~76,000 TR of projects set to commission and 76,782 TR of projects under implementation, with a broader pipeline of ~266,325 TR across real estate, airports, IT hubs, industrial estates, data centres and metro rail projects.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: AESL continued to scale its transmission platform during FY26, positioning itself as holding nearly one-fifth of India's private transmission network. Five transmission projects were commissioned during the year: Sangod Transmission, Khavda Phase-II Part-A and the Khavda Pooling Station-1 (commissioned in Q1), followed by additional network additions on the North Karanpura transmission line, culminating in the commissioning of the landmark Mumbai HVDC project (Mumbai's first advanced VSC-based HVDC installation). The company also secured the Khavda South Olpad HVDC line, reinforcing its position as the only private-sector player in India with HVDC capability. The transmission order book rose from Rs 59,936 crore to Rs 71,779 crore over the year. At the site/equipment level, the company commissioned a 12 Ohm series reactor in Mahendragarh, established a 4x500MVA, 400/220kV Jam Khambhaliya substation (GIS) in Gujarat under Jam Khambhaliya Transco Limited, and installed an additional 3.3 MW of solar capacity across Akola, Koradi, Mahendragarh, Rajnandangaon, Sami and Warangal sites (with Rs 0.43 crore capital investment on energy-conservation equipment during the year). Forward-looking strategic priorities identified include smart metering and digital grid expansion, development of green transmission corridors to evacuate renewable capacity, and strengthening internal capital classification/reporting to better track sustainability-linked R&D and capex spend in future reporting cycles.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- The **13,181 MU total handled vs 3,325 MU in the position book** is the tell: ~75% of throughput is low-margin services/trading. Do not extrapolate the ₹590cr EBIT off total volumes.
- **Adani Green does not sell to data centres at all** — it contracts long-term with SECI/DISCOMs/third parties. AESL is a *customer* of AGEL, and management confirmed that **essentially all group C&I exposure will route through Energy Solutions**, making AESL the group's single commercial front-end for C&I power.
- Management explicitly refused the analyst's arithmetic on 7.5 GW ("7.5 × 24 × 365") — it is a **market-opportunity number, not a contracted volume**, and mixes consumer stacks. Treat it as TAM framing.
- The smart-meter reporting inversion (accounting revenue falling while operating revenue more than doubles) will recur every quarter that installation pace slows — read the press release, not the presentation, for the annuity.

qoq_log.title: QoQ change log (fill each quarter)
qoq_log.body:
- **Q1FY27 (this):** Energy Solutions transitions from incubation to a full fourth vertical — ₹590cr EBIT, ~5 GW supply + 3,500 MWh BESS tied up, 350 MW C&I contracted. IntelliSmart acquisition announced (before CCI) taking pro-forma meters to ~4.7cr. 1.34cr meters installed cumulatively of 2.46cr. Quarterly capex ~₹3,500cr. HVDC dates set: KPS-1 ~Dec FY29, Rajasthan early FY29. Capex-addition guidance ₹20–25k cr/yr on ~25% market share. Parallel licence still frozen.
- _Q2FY27 → check: (a) how much of the 5 GW purchase position has been contracted back-to-back on the sale side, and at what spread; (b) whether Energy Solutions EBIT holds through the monsoon quarter; (c) CCI clearance for IntelliSmart; (d) smart-meter installation run-rate vs the 21-lakh Q1 number; (e) any STU order wins to validate the ₹20–25k cr/yr claim._
